en.title: New Blood CEO: 'Immersive Sim' is the Worst Way to Sell Games
en.summary: The CEO of **New Blood Interactive**, known for hits like **Dusk** and **Ultrakill**, believes the term 'immersive sim' actively harms the sales of beloved titles like **Gloomwood** and **Fallen Aces**. Dave Oshry argues that while fans adore the genre, marketing it with its own name is a losing battle.
en.body:
For fans of **Deus Ex**, **Dishonored**, and **Thief**, the term 'immersive sim' conjures images of intricate worlds, player freedom, and morally gray choices. It’s a label many wear with pride, a shorthand for a specific kind of deep, systems-driven gameplay. However, according to **Dave Oshry**, CEO of **New Blood Interactive**, it’s also one of the worst possible ways to actually sell these games.

**New Blood Interactive**, a company that cut its teeth on the retro-inspired boomer shooter revival with titles like **Dusk** and **Ultrakill**, has invested heavily in bringing two ambitious immersive sims, **Gloomwood** and **Fallen Aces**, to early access. Oshry humorously states he's "dumping all the money into immersive sims so we can go broke like the great studios that came before us, like Looking Glass," but his frank assessment of the marketability of the genre is no joke.

## The Marketing Minefield

Oshry admits he wasn't even familiar with the term 'immersive sim' until Dillon Rogers, the lead developer on **Gloomwood**, began working on the game. "He's like, 'That's what these are called'. I'm like, 'I have never heard that before in my life. What the fuck are you talking about?'" he recalls. Despite growing up with genre titans like **Deus Ex** and **Thief**, Oshry categorized them differently at the time. "Thief was a stealth game. I called it a stealth game. Deus Ex I called an FPS-RPG because it was an FPS, but it was an RPG. You had points that you put in stuff," he explained, likening the RPG elements to those found in **Diablo**.

This perspective highlights a key issue: the genre's defining characteristics, such as deep player progression and choice, have become more commonplace across various game types over the years. What once felt distinctly like an 'immersive sim' might now be seen as simply a well-designed RPG or a complex shooter.

## What This Means for Players

For the dedicated community that *does* understand and appreciate the nuances of immersive sims, this marketing hurdle presents a challenge. It means that potentially groundbreaking titles like **Gloomwood** and **Fallen Aces**, which offer the kind of emergent gameplay and player agency that fans crave, might struggle to find their audience if confined to a niche label. The success of these games, and by extension **New Blood Interactive**'s continued investment in the genre, hinges on finding a way to communicate their appeal beyond the established lexicon of hardcore fans. It’s a signal that innovation in how games are presented to the market is just as crucial as innovation within the games themselves.

## What's Next

**New Blood Interactive** continues to develop both **Gloomwood** and **Fallen Aces** in early access, with ongoing updates and refinements based on player feedback. Specific release windows for full versions have not yet been announced.

Yet there's something like consensus emerging among the makers of these games: it's really hard to sell an immersive sim while calling it by its name. "Is it a good marketing term? No," says New Blood Interactive CEO Dave Oshry. "It sucks. It's awful." (Image credit: New Blood) New Blood was first known for its boomer shooters, namely Dusk and Ultrakill , but has sunk years into two early access imsims, the well-regarded Gloomwood and Fallen Aces . Oshry likes to joke that he's "dumping all the money into immersive sims so we can go broke like the great studios that came before us, like Looking Glass." Yet he'd never heard the term immersive sim until Gloomwood lead Dillon Rogers started work on his Thief-and-Resi-riffing open world. "He's like, 'That's what these are called'. I'm like, 'I have never heard that before in my life. What the fuck are you talking about?'" Oshry wasn't new to the genre. He'd grown up adoring Deus Ex and Thief. "But Thief was a stealth game," he protests. "I called it a stealth game. Deus Ex I called an FPS-RPG because it was an FPS, but it was an RPG. You had points that you put in stuff. That's what an RPG is, like Diablo." (Image credit: New Blood) Of course, ploughing points into skills and traits is something that's proliferated across mainstream games of all kinds in the decades since. But it's true: back in the year 2000, it was largely the preserve of RPGs. Deus Ex, with its dialogue, narrative choices and deadly greasel combat seemed a natural enough addition to that genre. "System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs," Oshry says. "People called them RPGs. That's the funny thing about an immersive sim. You're immersed in this world. You're building your character. Yeah, that's called an RPG, brother. That's a roleplaying game." Does this age-old squabble over definitions really matter, so long as the games are good? Well, perhaps it does. Because immersive sims are considered to be niche and unworkable by many major publishers. Whereas RPGs? "They make lots of money and sell lots of copies," Oshry says. "You could argue that Baldur's Gate 3 is an immersive sim, because of the way that Larian builds their games. It's not first-person but you can stack boxes and use spells to pull things towards you and solve problems in unique ways." (Image credit: New Blood) The argument is one I've heard made before—in fact, I've even heard senior Larian developers refer to their Forgotten Realms opus as an immersive sim. But you won't find that phrase anywhere in its trailers or on its Steam page. "If you market something as an RPG, I think you'll do better than marketing it as an immersive sim," Oshry says.
